newsitem.title: KAZAKHSTAN: Kazakhstan sees more oil sell-offs in future.
newsitem.headline: Kazakhstan sees more oil sell-offs in future.

text.p: Oil-rich Kazakhstan has nearly completed privatising its largest oil companies but may still offer investors stakes in newly discovered oilfields, officials said on Friday.

The official Khabar news agency said on Friday the China National Petroleum Corp (CNPC) won exclusive rights to negotiate with Kazakhstan a deal to develop the Uzen oilfield, one of the ex-Soviet state's last big oil projects to be privatised.
"If within a month we agree on basic conditions, we will start preparing to sign a contract," Birzhan Madiyev, department head of the Finance Ministry's state property department told Reuters.
"One can say now that major oil projects are being completed," said Eduard Utepov, head of the Finance Ministry's privatisation department.
He added: "Kazakhstan has huge reserves of oil and it is possible that tomorrow a new large oilfield will be discovered and new tenders will be held."

Kazakhstan -- a vast Central Asian state five times the size of France and populated by just 16.7 million people -- has proven reserves of 2.8 billion tonnes of oil and 1.7 trillion cubic meters of natural gas.
But industry experts say these may be just a fraction of total reserves.

Officials hope a massive influx of cash from foreign investors will allow Kazakhstan to steady the recession-battered economy, modernise the oil industry and become one of the world's largest oil producers.

In the case of Uzen, located in western Kazakhstan near the Caspian Sea and exploited since 1965, the government hopes eventually to return to the field's former annual yield of 16 million tonnes (320,000 bpd) last recorded in 1975.
Output at Uzen, with estimated proven reserves of over 200 million tonnes, is 2.7 million tonnes (54,000 bpd).
Madiyev said that Kazakhstan and CNPC could agree to set up a joint venture on a production-sharing basis.

He declined to name the sum of investment needed to rehabilitate one of Kazakhstan's oldest fields, but said the minimum investment from CNPC should be no less than $400 million. But it could reach $1 billion.

In May this year Indonesia's Central Asia Petroleum Ltd, part-owned by Indonesia's Medco Energy Corp and Sedtco Group, bought a 60-percent stake in Kazakhstan's largest oil producer Mangistaumunaigaz for a total of $4.348 billion, pledging to invest $2 billion in the first five years.
In June CNPC won a tender for a 60-percent stake in another large producer, Aktobemunaigaz, for a total of $4.325 billion.

U.S. oil majors Chevron and Mobil have already invested hundreds of millions of dollars in their joint venture on the giant Tengiz field in western Kazakhstan, with proven reserves of 6-9 billion barrels.
Officials say that their policy of attracting investors is already yielding fruit.

"Investment commitments in projects to develop oil fields are estimated at $32.3 billion, while projects for exploration of hydrocarbons are worth $8.2 billion," Nurlan Balgimbayev, head of the state company Kazakh Oil, told the economic weekly Delovaya Nedelya on Friday.

"In the last three years over $3 billion was invested in these projects -- the lion's share of all direct investment in the republic. We have every chance to become a recognised oil power in the world," he added.
Balgimbayev says that Kazakhstan plans to boost its oil production to 170 million tonnes (3.4 million bpd) by the year 2010 from some 27 million tonnes (540,000 bpd) this year.
